debit_pay_findings.evidence: Wiki lists working debit/prepaid BINs (Alaska/SunTrust/UFB Direct debit, Green Dot, H&R Block Emerald, PayPal Business MC, Simple, Swagbucks, Wells Fargo) vs failing ones (Amex gift/debit, Bluebird, Serve, Chase Starbucks Prepaid, US Bank Visa Buxx, Vanilla). debit_pay_findings.limit_note: no debit-card leg exists; phone/online payment requires a linked checking/savings account (ACH) only
debit_pay_findings.evidence: Capital One's own help-center content and third-party guides confirm debit-card and other-credit-card payments are not accepted toward a Capital One credit card bill; ACH from a bank account, mail, or in-person are the only funding rails.

debit_pay_findings.limit_note: no debit-card leg exists; phone payment requires a bank routing/account number
debit_pay_findings.evidence: Amex does not accept a debit card as a bill-payment instrument by any direct channel; phone payment requires entering a bank account and routing number, not a card number. Indirect debit routing is only possible through a third-party biller like doxo.

debit_pay_findings.cards: store cards (JCPenney, HSN, Sam's Club, etc.)
debit_pay_findings.limit_note: direct debit-card payment via 'Pay as Guest'/'Pay Without Log In'; another credit card is not accepted
debit_pay_findings.evidence: Synchrony's own site offers a guest-payment flow that explicitly takes a debit card or bank account; phone payment with a rep can also take a debit card. Third-party biller doxo is a separate, fee-bearing route.

debit_pay_findings.channel: store register (Sam's Club or Walmart) / phone / online
debit_pay_findings.limit_note: cash/debit at register gives immediate open-to-buy restoration vs 7-14 day hold for checks; register no longer takes payment at the Membership Desk, must use checkout register; Direct Credit accounts must pay by mail only
debit_pay_findings.evidence: Sam's Club support pages confirm in-person debit/cash payment at any Sam's Club or Walmart register posts instantly; store-card-at-register payment is one of the clearest 'pay a credit-style card at a register with a debit card' patterns the MS community watches for.

debit_pay_findings.cards: third-party in-person bill pay network, used to fund many credit-card issuers' bills
debit_pay_findings.limit_note: network is built around cash/debit; direct credit-card funding of the bill is generally not supported, cash and debit are the emphasized rails
debit_pay_findings.evidence: CheckFreePay is described as the largest US in-person bill-payment processor; it can post payment to nearly any Visa/Mastercard-issued credit card bill, but the FUNDING side (what you pay WITH) is cash/debit-oriented, not itself a credit card.

debit_pay_findings.cards: bill-pay to registered billers, including credit cards
debit_pay_findings.limit_note: debit card linked to a US bank (or direct bank transfer) is treated as non-cash-advance and is the cost-effective route; fee varies by biller/amount
debit_pay_findings.evidence: Western Union's own bill-pay FAQ states debit-card funding avoids the cash-advance fee/interest that a credit card funding source would trigger, making it a candidate 'debit funds credit-card bill' rail.

debit_pay_findings.cards: bill-pay to 13,000+ registered billers including credit cards
debit_pay_findings.limit_note: credit-card funding of a MoneyGram bill payment can trigger a cash-advance fee/interest from the card issuer; debit-card funding avoids that
debit_pay_findings.evidence: MoneyGram accepts Visa/Mastercard/Discover/Diners/UnionPay debit or credit as funding, or cash in person; the community-relevant path is debit-funds-credit-card-bill to avoid the cash-advance flag that a credit-funds-credit-card leg would create.

debit_pay_findings.cards: in-store bill pay to many billers including credit cards
debit_pay_findings.limit_note: MoneyCenter is cash/debit-only for funding; no credit-card funding accepted at the counter
debit_pay_findings.evidence: Walmart's MoneyCenter explicitly serves 'cash-preferred and underbanked' customers who pay bills (including credit cards) with cash or a debit card; this is a straightforward debit-funds-any-credit-card-bill channel with no fee data captured.

debit_pay_findings.cards: pays any billed vendor/credit-card style bill
debit_pay_findings.limit_note: flagged per prompt instructions: Plastiq funds a payment FROM a credit card (a credit rail), and separately offers ~1% debit-card funding that explicitly earns NO card rewards on the funding leg — so it does not stack Taekus rewards the way a native debit bill-pay channel would
debit_pay_findings.evidence: 2026-era Plastiq pricing: ~2.9% flat fee to fund a payment with a credit card, or ~1% to fund with a debit card but with no points/rewards earned on that debit leg — makes it unsuitable for the debit-rewards-stacking play described in the task.

new_card_leads.why_interesting: 4% back on APMEX purchases via waitlist card, but APMEX adds a credit-card surcharge that DoctorOfCredit says largely offsets the 4%

ms_criteria.what_they_look_for: An account frozen/flagged by the issuer for review, usually triggered by abnormal spending behavior relative to the cardholder's normal profile
ms_criteria.why: An FR can freeze pending rewards/points and block further spend, so the community treats avoiding FR triggers as a primary risk-management goal

ms_criteria.what_they_look_for: Chase auto-denies new-card applicants with 5+ new accounts (any issuer) opened in the trailing 24 months; the community times applications around this and similar issuer-specific velocity rules
ms_criteria.why: Velocity of NEW ACCOUNTS (not just spend) is itself a risk signal issuers and the community both track, separate from spend-based shutdown risk

ms_criteria.what_they_look_for: Using a rewards card to buy cash-equivalents (gift cards, money orders, prepaid loads, gold bars) that can be liquidated back to cash/bill-pay near face value, to earn rewards without real net spend
ms_criteria.why: This is the core mechanic the whole community optimizes; net cost = fees + spread - rewards, and the entire evaluation framework is built around minimizing that net cost per dollar of spend

ms_criteria.what_they_look_for: Deliberately keeping cash-equivalent transactions under the $10,000 CTR reporting threshold to avoid a Currency Transaction Report is itself a federal crime (structuring), regardless of whether the underlying funds are legitimate; banks that spot patterns must file a Suspicious Activity Report (SAR)
ms_criteria.why: High-volume/high-dollar MS (like $10k-50k/month gold buys) is exactly the profile that risks tripping CTR/SAR-adjacent scrutiny if payment patterns look designed to stay under thresholds

ms_criteria.what_they_look_for: US Bank (and its Elan-issued partner cards) are described by the community as broadly MS-unfriendly, with cross-product bans once one card is shut down
ms_criteria.why: One user reported denial on a US Bank Smartly application specifically because of a prior Fidelity 2% (Elan-issued) card shutdown, i.e. 'Elan is owned by US Bank and they levied a ban for all products' — issuer-family-wide blacklisting, not just single-card

ms_criteria.topic: Amex shutdown rumblings tied to specific apps/services
ms_criteria.what_they_look_for: Community monitors real-time 'shutdown wave' reports and tries to attribute the trigger (e.g. a specific third-party cashback app) rather than assuming general MS caused it
ms_criteria.why: Attributing shutdown waves to a specific app/service (here, 'Fluz-related') lets the community keep using other channels while avoiding the flagged one

ms_criteria.what_they_look_for: Community view (msp3, responding to hotpancakes' question about Costco gold-bar shutdown risk) is that risk scales with behaviors like maxing out per-membership order limits repeatedly and using deferred-interest/pay-over-time financing (e.g. Chase Pay Over Time) on large gold purchases, more than the raw dollar volume itself
ms_criteria.why: Distinguishes 'large legitimate purchase' from 'pattern that looks like spend gaming' in the issuer's eyes — maxing limits + financing large purchases reads as manufactured/abusive even if gold itself isn't excluded

ms_criteria.what_they_look_for: The community watches for a merchant's MCC reclassification, a card's terms rewrite, or a newly added spend cap as the concrete events that kill a play, more than any specific dollar threshold
ms_criteria.why: A play dies not from being 'too large' in the abstract but from a specific, datable coding/terms change (e.g. an issuer excluding MCC 5300 from a bonus category, or a debit BIN losing IVR compatibility) — hence the community's obsession with dated, BIN/MCC-specific data points over general advice

gold_costco_notes.note: Costco is MCC 5300 (Wholesale Club); most cards' 'grocery' bonus categories explicitly EXCLUDE Superstores/Warehouse Clubs, so gold at Costco earns only the card's generic/base rate unless the card has a Costco-specific bonus

Stacking play the community describes: Costco Executive Membership's 2% annual reward (capped) on qualifying purchases including gold, PLUS the card's own cash back (e.g. Costco Anywhere Visa by Citi 2%), reported to reach up to ~4% combined effective back on a gold purchase

In-warehouse Costco register is Visa-only; Costco.com accepts Visa and Mastercard, which shapes which card can even be used for the buy leg (relevant to non-Visa MS workarounds like buying then returning)

Community risk framing (FlyerTalk Shutdown Thread, Jan 2025): buying gold bars at Costco itself isn't flagged as inherently dangerous; risk instead comes from maxing per-membership order limits repeatedly and using deferred/pay-over-time financing (e.g. Chase Pay Over Time) on large gold purchases

Non-Costco bullion-dealer data point: one dealer added a 2% credit-card surcharge on gold purchases, which can fully offset a 2% rewards card's earn — the 'no free money' warning applies broadly to bullion MS, not just Costco

Resale/unwind economics warning repeated across sources: gold markets are efficient, dealer bid/ask spreads (one data point: ~5% buy/sell spread on a common 1oz coin) and platform fees on resale can erase the card-rewards margin unless spot price also moves favorably between buy and sell

No FlyerTalk/community source found in this sweep that states Costco gold bars carry an explicit per-membership unit cap in the MS threads themselves (retail listings elsewhere show per-drop limits like 'max 5 units' on some bar sizes, but that's retail stock-limiting, not a card-issuer rule)

taekus_notes.note: Taekus operates on an interchange-share model across personal/business/corporate prepaid debit products; its issuing bank (Stearns Bank NA, program manager GoGreen FI LLC) reportedly has under $10B in assets, exempting it from the Durbin interchange cap, which the community cites as the structural reason it can pay outsized debit rewards

myFICO thread reports HIGHLY VARIABLE real-world reward rates by merchant type: an Amazon reload earned 0% cash back, misc purchases 'very little', but a hotel purchase earned about 2% — no single headline rate confirmed, and no post in this sweep confirmed rewards specifically posting on a credit-card BILL-PAYMENT transaction

Described elsewhere as supporting a 'micropayments' mechanism where a 14-cent transaction reportedly nets a 9-cent rebate — an extreme, likely edge-case/promotional data point rather than the sustained effective rate on normal-sized spend; treat as unverified/anecdotal

myFICO moderator/participants describe Taekus as 'shadowy' and invite-only, flagging skepticism due to its small total funding (~$6-6.4M) relative to competitor fintechs — a caution about counterparty/longevity risk, not a confirmed shutdown

No thread found in this sweep (FlyerTalk, myFICO, DoctorOfCredit, FrequentMiler, or search-surfaced Reddit content) that explicitly states whether Taekus rewards are excluded as an AFT (MCC 6012/6051) when used to fund a credit-card bill payment specifically, nor any documented monthly/per-transaction reward cap — this remains an open question after the sweep
